#197. Trump wooed Latino voters, but his ICE tactics sent them back to the polls: ‘They’re taking our neighbors’

Texas business owner says he expected ICE raids to focus on those with criminal records not his relatives and employees

Tuesday night’s explosive rout of the Republican party was supercharged by the fury of Hispanic Americans who turned out in record numbers in key battlegrounds to protest the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant assault on their communities.

“Trump went against us,” said Benny Melendez from Weslaco, Texas. “He made us the target of ICE operations, so we decided to punish him by voting against his party. That’s what happened.”

Melendez, the owner of a small housebuilding company in south Texas, voted for Donald Trump in the presidential election two years ago, attracted by his promise to secure the Mexican border and improve the economy. But on Tuesday, he cast his vote for the Democrats in a display of pure anger.

Two of his cousins and up to 15 of his building workers have been picked up and deported to Mexico by ICE. When Melendez voted for Trump in 2024 he expected the immigration raids would focus on those with criminal records, he said, not his relatives and employees.

“They’re taking our neighbors. They’re taking our friends. They’re they’re taking our workers, and they’re taking our family members. This is an attack against our community.”

Melendez’s rage, replicated in the millions across Texas, Florida and other critical swing states, itself tells a story. It speaks to how Trump first wooed, and then alienated, the backing of many Latino voters, effectively shooting himself in the foot.

In the closing days of the 2024 presidential race, Trump made a special pitch to Hispanic voters. “I love Hispanics,” he told them, “and Hispanics love Trump.”

To some extent, that audacious appeal worked: in 2024 Trump garnered 48% of the Latino vote, according to Pew Research, 12 points up from four years previously.

But on Tuesday night, Latino voters delivered Trump a resounding message of a very different sort. In a dizzying switch in affiliation, Hispanic American support for Republicans plummeted from the almost half who backed Trump just two years ago to 30% today.

According to the New York Times analysis of voter trends, election night marked a 28 point shift from 2024 in Latino allegiance toward Democrats nationwide. The dramatic turn was more notable than any other demographic voting group, with the next largest shift of 17% coming from Asian Americans.

The shift helped propel Democratic wins in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, as well as governor’s seats in states like Texas, Georgia, Arizona and Nevada.

If Trump and the Republican party had assumed they had forged a new alignment with Hispanic voters, they must now think again. Any such alliance was abruptly and spectacularly uncoupled on Tuesday.

“People have called us the sleeping giant for a long time, and now we’re really the swinging giant,” said Stephanie Valencia, co-founder of the Latino polling experts, Equis Research.

“The vociferous message that voters sent last night was an F-U to Trump and Republicans and their misplaced priorities and broken promises.”

It was a night of stunning surprises, and of firsts. Texas, the state with the second largest Hispanic populace after California, elected its first Latino governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a native of the Rio Grande Valley whose mother is an immigrant from Mexico, in an astounding rebuke to decades of largely white Republican rule.

Democrat Xavier Becerra, the son of immigrants from Mexico, will become the first elected Latino governor in California, the world’s fourth largest economy.

Here too the same voters’ fury was powerfully vented. “We’ve known better than anybody what these last two years have been like,” California senator Alex Padilla, the son of Mexican immigrants, told the crowd at Becerra’s closing campaign stop at the Palladium in Los Angeles on Sunday. “We have endured relentless attacks on our communities by Donald Trump and his rogue ICE agents.”

Angelica Salas, an immigration activist who leads the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles, called Becerra “familia”.

“Xavier Becerra dreams the way we dream,” she said.

In key battleground states, Latino voters flexed their electoral muscle in this midterm cycle to a degree arguably never seen before. Texas took the prize for the seismic jolt that shot across the state.

In Hispanic-dominated south Texas where Trump made some of his greatest gains two years ago, Democrats won all four congressional districts along the border with Mexico. That included the three districts that Republicans had gerrymandered in an attempt to bolster their control of the US House – a move that backfired.

Two of those districts were held by their Democratic incumbents, Henry Cuellar in Texas 28 and Vicente Gonzalez in Texas 34. The third gerrymandered district, 81% Hispanic Texas 15, was flipped by the Democratic candidate, the Tejano music star Bobby Pulido.

Pulido always looked to be doing well against the Republican incumbent, Monica De La Cruz, even though Trump had prevailed here in 2024. In the end, Pulido’s victory was overwhelming, by an astonishing 24 percentage points with 95% of the ballots counted.

“Not bad for a quinceañera singer,” Pulido said at his victory event.

Pulido’s campaign manager Abel Prado told the Guardian that the outstanding result was in part a reflection of Trump’s mass deportation drive that has seen thousands of undocumented Hispanic people detained and deported by ICE in Texas. “When you implement policies with such cruelty and malice, then this is what you get,” Prado said.

Among the 48,000 individuals that the Pulido campaign assembled in its voter database, almost 40% they found were members of mixed-status families. “These are people whose parents couldn’t vote, but they could, and so when my dad got deported, or my mom got deported, that became a crystallizing moment.”

Prado said that many people in the district who had voted for Trump in 2024 “came to their senses and realized the consequences of their previous vote. Tuesday night was a correction to what happens when one party is allowed to run rampant and do whatever they want without fear of consequences.”

The 30 million registered Latino voters are as diverse politically, culturally and economically as any other group. Talk of a Latino monolith has for years led analysts to reach simplistic and inaccurate conclusions about their voting patterns.

Yet Tuesday’s results showed a surprisingly similar rejection of Trump’s policies across very different Hispanic communities. In Florida, Latino voters swung powerfully toward Democratic candidates in the Cuban and Venezuelan communities of Miami-Dade, and equally in the heavily Puerto Rican areas around Orlando.

In Miami-Dade, which Trump won by a whopping 15 points in 2024, the Republican incumbent Maria Elvira Salazar was fighting a neck-and-neck battle with her fellow Cuban American newscaster, the Democratic candidate Eliott Rodriguez.

That the race was so tight amounted to the realisation of Salazar’s worst fears. In September she was blasted over news headlines when she warned Trump in a campaign advert that his mass deportation of Hispanic immigrants had “gone too far” and that the very people who had put him back in the White House now “feel betrayed”.

Trump’s response was indicative. He accused Salazar of backstabbing him, claiming that his “Latino support hasn’t wavered.” The voters disagreed.

Tuesday’s results will reverberate for some time. Democratic leaders, as they prepare to take control of Congress and begin the search for a presidential nominee, should be mindful that Hispanic voters are hungry for policies that reflect their needs, Valencia said.

“This was a cry for help from voters to focus on the right things: the economy and inflation, immigration, and wars abroad. Democrats are entering a probationary period with voters, they should not make the mistake of thinking that this swing is permanent.”

The election has also ushered in a new generation of young, ambitious Hispanic politicians and organizers determined to be heard. Pulido’s entire campaign staff was aged under 25.

“These are people who have never had a seat at the table who can now become a new voice in how we do things,” Prado said. “We absolutely rejected anybody parachuting into the district, out-of-towners telling us how to do things.”

He added: “If there’s a gringo operative out there trying to take credit for what happened to the Latino vote in Texas on Tuesday night, please shut the fuck up.”

Tesla will stop making the Cybertruck next year, according to CEO Elon Musk, who said on X that the company will use the factory space to build more two-seater Cybercab robotaxis.

The decision to wind down the futuristic, steel-clad EV comes after just a few short years of underwhelming sales. When Musk handed over the first few Cybertrucks in late 2023, he predicted Tesla would sell around 250,000 per year. It was supposed to be such a cornerstone of Tesla’s future that, before construction began, the company talked about its Texas factory as the “Cybertruck factory.” But Tesla has instead sold just tens of thousands — total — over the last three years.

Tesla is killing off the Cybertruck at a moment when it is trying to become an AI- and robotics-focused company. A big part of that is its robotaxi ambitions.

The company has spent the last two months putting Cybercabs on the streets in its hometown of Austin, Texas. With no major incidents to date, the company has said it plans to expand the Cybercabs operations to other cities, starting with Dallas later this month. (Tesla also operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUVs in Austin, Houston, and Dallas, as well as three cities in Florida.)

This is the third product Tesla has discontinued in order to fuel those greater ambitions. Earlier this year, the company decided to end production of the Model S sedan and Model X SUV and instead use the factory space dedicated to those vehicles to make Optimus humanoid robots.

First announced in 2019, the Cybertruck was a product that Musk had long obsessed over.

“Probably my personal favorite for the next product is the pickup truck, and we are going to just do an amazing pickup truck,” he said on one of Tesla’s earnings calls that year.

Musk promised the Cybertruck would be radical, inspired by the designs of cyberpunk sci-fi stories like Blade Runner. While that certainly bore out in the design, the company overpromised on the basics of the Cybertruck from the jump. During the now-infamous reveal event in 2019, when head designer Franz von Holzhausen cracked the Cybertruck’s windows with steel balls, Tesla said the EV was supposed to start at under $40,000 and have up to 500 miles of range. It achieved neither of those figures.

Instead, the truck was delayed for two years, in part because of the Covid-19 pandemic. When it finally did hit the market in late 2023, Tesla handed over the first few Cybertrucks to customers in a short, somewhat odd for Tesla event (by the company’s own standards, at least), which saw a poorly-lit Musk standing in a truck bed promising the truck was “the finest in apocalyptic equipment” fit for “late civilization vibes.” The base price had inflated to around $60,000, and the top-end range had shrunk by over 100 miles.

The truck has struggled on the market ever since. The polarizing design never seemed to sit well with buyers, especially at a higher-than-expected price. Then, during its first full year of sales in 2024, Musk became a major financial backer of Donald Trump, which turned the instantly recognizable Cybertruck into a target for protesters. That continued into 2025 as Musk led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, which fired thousands of federal workers.

#195. New bomb threats target Irish media, more flights

Newsrooms have been evacuated across Ireland after another wave of bomb threats. Dublin is hosting a high-level EU meeting in several days.

Following days of bomb threats grounding flights across Europe, media institutions in Ireland were added to the list of targets on Friday.

Irish public broadcaster Raidio Teilifis Eirean (RTE) said that its buildings had been evacuated after receiving a bomb threat. Other media organizations were also taking security measures.

The threats come two days before Dublin, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, hosts a high-level meeting with other bloc members.

An RTE reporter said the group that claimed to be behind Friday's bomb threats was the same that had sent threats to airlines earlier in the week.

"We don't yet know whether it's an individual behind this effort, or some form of a co-ordinated effort," Irish Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris told Cork 96FM radio.

He said it was a "serious and evolving situation."

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin called the developments "worrying," but said the Gardai (Irish police) and Defense Forces were looking into who was behind the threats.

He also urged any organization that receives a similar threat to take it seriously and report it to the police so they can have a "picture of what's happening."

"It just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause disruption, designed to cause fear and anxiety," RTE cited Martin as saying.

Asked about any possible connection with the European Union meetings coming up in Dublin, the prime minister, also known as the Taoiseach, said it was important to maintain the ability to let such meetings go ahead.

"We have the largest number of prime ministers ever at the one time in our country, and that does call for very significant security operations."

More than two dozen flights were affected by threats this week, with further incidents reported on Friday.

Police in Denmark and the Czech Republic responded to threats that ultimately proved to be false.

A flight operated by the Romanian carrier Tarom going from Prague to Bucharest received a threat, but landed at its intended destination before officials deemed it false.

Police in Copenhagen said they had been to the airport for the second day in a row "in connection with threats directed at air traffic" but that there had been no danger to passengers or disruption to flights.

While bomb threats are not uncommon, such a wave of threats being made in a short period of time is unusual, especially amid increasing geopolitical tensions with Russia and a wave of hybrid attacks that have brought disruption to Europe.

#191. Physicl raises $10M to make the digital world real enough for robots

Alex de Vigan’s last business got swamped by the rise of generative AI, but now he’s betting the tech that team had built, a platform for creating tempting product renderings for e-commerce, can be re-purposed to make robots more useful.

His new venture, Physicl, has raised $10 million in seed funding from Inovia Capital to help world model designers and robot builders solve thorny training problems with more realistic simulations.

Founder and CEO de Vigan spent the last decade building nfinite, which made it easy for brands and retailers to create 3D models of their goods and display them online. The arrival of transformer-based AI models led that company to focus more on generative imagery, but de Vigan saw a new purpose for his team and the tech stack they’d built to faithfully render 3D environments.

“What we were super unique about doing in 3D, AI was going to replace, but something was missing in AI: its ability to understand, interact, and manipulate space and objects,” de Cigan says.

Researchers developing physical AI models to make robots more capable of tasks like handling diverse, small objects have been frustrated by the returns of training them on video, and the expense of gathering data through remote operations.

Simulations in digital worlds are seen as a promising solution, but ensuring that these simulated worlds are faithful to real-world physics has proven difficult. de Vigan believes that the pipeline his previous company built to “transform unstructured, incomplete, heterogeneous real-world information into a high-fidelity physical representation… with correct geometry, materials, and physics” can now be used to make physical AI models more effective.

Physcl is entering a crowded category of startups vying to provide data and tooling to foundation model builders and robot operators. “The space is very young and and and very blurry sometimes,” de Vigan admits. There are a variety of companies collecting, labeling, or generating data in different modalities as their customers try to figure out the secret sauce that will make robots live up to their promise.

In particular, Phyiscl wants to focus on post-training models on difficult edge cases. The startup is releasing a product called Studio with 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 assets that represent various objects. It lets users create scenes to generate synthetic data for training robots on specific problems. For example, Studio could be used to generate training data to help a robot that has trouble discerning a cup on a cluttered counter-top, or while the cup is in shadow.

SpAItial, a world model builder, collaborated with Physicl as an early customer to improve the fidelity of its products, the latest of which, Echo-3, was released last week. SpAItial’s tool generates 3D simulations from 2D imagery, and to do that effectively, its CEO and founder Matthias Niessner said they needed to train on the kind of high-fidelity synthetic data Physicl offers.

However, Physicl wants to be more than a data provider; it sees itself as the tooling for ongoing synthetic data generation. “What we created 10 years ago, without knowing it, was basically an agentic workflow to transform unstructured information into high fidelity 3D,” de Vigan said. He imagines customers bringing trillions of images or millions of hours of LIDAR capture data to feed into his platform and turn them into high-quality 3D representations that can be used to generate billions of permutations to train their models.

“The real challenge is, you have to curate the data by hand, and this is a very long cycle,” Niessner, also a professor of robotics at the Technical University of Munich, told TechCrunch. “To us what seems very attractive is you can just do this on the fly […] You’re running Claude, and it checks, ‘Oh, I need more data of this in my training,’ and then it auto generates that data, depending on the training state. That, to me, is super exciting, and this is exactly what Physicl is offering.”

#190. ‘An abomination’: Idaho hunters earned thousands of dollars to kill newborn wolf pups, records reveal

Wildlife advocates incensed as documents show state paid out $2,000 per kill in effort to shrink state’s wolf population

Idaho officials paid hunters thousands of dollars for killing a dozen newborn wolf pups this spring, including what appears to be at least one full litter killed in or near its den, according to state records shared with the Guardian and Public Domain.

The wolf pup killings have incensed wildlife advocates in Idaho, where state wildlife officials have been ordered to take extraordinary measures to shrink the state’s re-introduced wolf population amid complaints from the livestock industry and big game hunting outfitters.

A law passed five years ago by the Republican-dominated state legislature loosened restrictions on hunting seasons, removed restrictions on killing methods and allowed people to contract third parties to kill wolves. Individual hunters and trappers are able to buy an unlimited number of permits to kill wolves, which cost $14 each for state residents and $32 for non-residents.

In 2021, Idaho game officials also entered into an agreement with the Foundation for Wildlife Management, a non-profit devoted to reducing wolves to help boost deer and elk numbers, to reimburse expenses to any hunter and trapper who provides proof of killing a wolf. The program pays for a wide range of expenses, including truck payments, fuel, ammunition and outdoor clothing.

The reimbursement program paid $2,000 per wolf kill through the hunting season that ended in June, including the 12 pups, records from the state’s fish and game agency show. The program is funded with a mix of taxpayer money, hunting license sales and contributions from the Foundation for Wildlife Management. .

“It’s an abomination,” said Brooks Fahy, director of the advocacy group Predator Defense. “I think most people, even in Idaho, if they actually understood the depth of this, the fact that taxpayer dollars are paying for this – they would be appalled.”

“Let’s call this what it is – it’s a goddamned bounty,” Fahy said. “What kind of receipts are you going to show for 12 pups who weigh 12lbs? It’s ridiculous on its face and the state of Idaho should be ashamed.”

Neither the foundation nor the Idaho wolf depredation control board, a government entity that oversees payments for third-party wolf killings, responded to requests for comment.

Gray wolves were all but wiped off the map in the continental United States by the mid-20th century through government extermination programs, but the population has rebounded in Idaho since being reintroduced by the US Fish and Wildlife Service in 1995. That has reignited tensions with ranchers and big game outfitters whose livelihoods are affected by the animals.

Three separate hunters used rifles to kill a total of 12 wolf pups in Idaho’s northern panhandle region on April 25, the records show – though in at least two instances the records also include a contradictory statement saying that “no weapon” was used. The pups were likely between one and three weeks old by that date. Wolves give birth once a year in the spring.

Hunters and trappers must present a skull and hide with proof of sex attached to a wildlife officer for every wolf killed in the state. The officer normally takes a tooth sample, which allows state biologists to estimate the animal’s age and genetic information.

Officers did not take teeth samples from the 12 pups, however – likely because their teeth had yet to grow in or were too small to extract, according to Idaho fish and game biologist Cory Mosby.

Mosby confirmed that the 12 wolves documented in the records were pups. No state regulation bars the killing of pups, he said. Wildlife officials would normally restrict killing pups by closing the hunting and trapping seasons during the spring, when wolves typically give birth.

But the state management plan, adopted in 2023, mandates culling wolves to about 650 animals in spring, when wolf numbers typically peak. The state’s permissive hunting and trapping regulations, including the yearlong season, are designed to tamp wolf numbers down to that target and will likely become more restrictive as the population dwindles, Mosby said.

That day remains a long way away. Idaho wildlife authorities estimate that the population peaked at about 1,600 wolves in spring back in 2019. That figure for this year still stood at more than 1,100 wolves, despite aggressive hunting and trapping and state-backed payments to incentivize wolf killings. Mosby said that hitting the target would require consistently killing more than a third of the wolf population annually.

“They’re an incredibly impressive and resilient species,” Mosby said. “It takes sustained, high levels of harvest to get into what you call ‘additive’ mortality – where you’re actually removing animals.”

The records state that all 12 wolf pups were killed by “still stalk” – a method in which hunters spot an animal and then sneak up on it to take a shot.

But wolf experts said that the hunters responsible had more likely located the dens, monitored them until the mothers had given birth, then pulled the pups out to kill them.

The tactic of fishing wild canine pups from dens has a long history in the American west, where livestock interests have historically clashed with wolves and coyotes. Modern trail cameras with cellular technology make it far easier to watch over dens, said Carter Niemeyer, who spent nearly three decades working at the US Department of Agriculture’s wildlife services, an agency charged with lethal removal of animals that prey on livestock.

“Killing six wolves or 12 wolves total all on the same day by stalking – that doesn’t happen,” Niemeyer said. “Never heard of it.”

“It would be easy to determine when a female had her pups by her physical appearance going in and out of her den,” Niemeyer added. “I think the public should be outraged by it and sportsmen should be outraged by it too. I’m a sportsman and that’s stooping pretty low – collecting bounties on wolf pups.”

Doug Smith, a biologist who oversaw the wolf program at Yellowstone national park, said he has pulled wolf pups out of dens for research purposes. The parents don’t usually protect their young. Instead, they scurry off about 50 yards away and bark.

“It’s easy to do,” Smith said. “If you can’t reach them, you dig them out with a shovel.”

Smith raised concerns about killing whole litters, however. Wolves travel more independently in the summer and use the den to regroup later in the year. Killing a whole litter could fracture a pack or dissolve it entirely, he said.

“Wolves breed once a year, so the birth of the pups is a very important thing,” Smith said. “The pack’s life hinges on those pups. They’re the glue that holds the pack together.”

Gray wolves remain protected by the Endangered Species Act in most of the continental United States. But the northern Rocky states of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming have all secured state management of wolves since their reintroduction to the region in the 1990s. All three states have pursued aggressive tactics to beat their numbers back.

Idaho hunters and trappers have targeted wolf pups in the past. Hunters killed three pups with rifle shots in the same region two years ago, according to a report from the Idaho Statesman. Federal wildlife control officers killed eight wolf pups from Idaho’s Timberline pack outside Boise back in 2021 to avoid conflict with a rancher, drawing condemnation from wolf advocates, environmental groups and local students who had adopted the pack as their high school mascot.

But advocates view the continuing trend as more worrisome in light of Donald Trump’s recent moves against wolves. In September, Trump signed an executive order encouraging the interior department to consider stripping gray wolves of their Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections across the continental United States – despite the fact that ESA protections for gray wolves remain tied up in federal litigation.

At the signing ceremony, Trump appeared to ask an Arizona rancher whether his new order allowed people to kill Mexican gray wolves, a sub-species in the south-west that is also federally protected.

“You can shoot them as of today?” Trump asked.

The crowd laughed. US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins responded that interior secretary Doug Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes” – despite the fact that Mexican gray wolves remain ESA-protected and have not come close to meeting de-listing requirements.

Another rancher at the ceremony told Trump about his struggles with wolves in the state of Washington.

“You’re allowed to go and take care of it,” Trump said.

“If you say so, sir,” the rancher responded.

“We have no choice,” Trump said. “I’ve been hearing about it for a long time.”

“Trump says you can go out and kill wolves now – how many people took him at his word?” said Fahy, the wolf advocate. “These are sentient creatures. They’re basically dogs. They form family bonds. They mate for life, pretty much. They have a pack structure that is very similar to our social structure. How could we be so wantonly cruel to something that is so similar to us?”

#189. Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo

AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.

One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.

The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.

You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.

We made a game for our new frontier text-to-speech model, Woof. 31.7 MB, so small that it runs in your browser Play the game on X… all voices are Woof. Defeat Darkcloud for an invite https://t.co/ImUFYDCBQG pic.twitter.com/tthHx7ZGBK

You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.

All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.

While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.

This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark, a 167 MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.

Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog, told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.

“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto.

In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally-hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.

#188. Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI

Decision made in order for factory in Texas to be used for Cybercab, the carmaker’s self-driving taxi

Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking the end of a failed effort to take a chunk of the lucrative market for pickups in the US.

The billionaire chief executive said production of the car would stop in about the middle of next year at the company’s factory in Texas in order to use the plant for the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.

Musk did not say whether Tesla had plans to produce the vehicle in another factory, although that would probably require significant investment for the specialised tooling needed to make it.

Musk has pinned hopes for Tesla on robotics, artificial intelligence and an autonomous driving fleet rather than following the traditional carmakers’ approach of developing a steady stream of new models to entice private buyers.

It caps a tricky week for the world’s richest person, after Republican candidates he had backed with $446m (£332m) in donations lost in the US midterm elections. The paper value of Musk’s fortune fell by $113bn after the extent of the rout became clear, as stock market investors questioned whether a Democrat-led Congress could slow the pace of the AI boom.

Tesla shares fell by 11% on Thursday, while his AI and rocket launch company, SpaceX, dropped by 9%.

Tesla started deliveries of the Cybertruck in late 2023, after several long delays as the company tried to cope with the technical challenges of producing such an unusual vehicle – and particularly its steel shell.

The Cybertruck never made it on sale in Europe because it did not reach the required safety standards.

Even before sales began, Musk acknowledged how difficult it would be to make it a success. In a 2023 earnings call, he said: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck,” and noted “enormous challenges” in increasing production and earning money from it.

Musk had said the company aimed to sell 200,000 Cybertrucks each year but it never approached that target. Tesla does not report sales of the trucks separately but in the third quarter of 2026 it delivered only 8,300 “other models”, which include the Cybertruck. The vast majority of its sales were the Model 3 saloon and the Model Y SUV, with 478,000 combined deliveries during the quarter.

Tesla also this year stopped production of its Model S and Model X, its premium saloon and SUV, amid declining sales for ageing products.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

Tesla’s automotive focus has shifted to the Cybercab. Tesla has started offering paid trips in the car, which has space for two passengers and no steering wheel, in limited parts of Austin, Texas. However, it is unclear how quickly the company will be able to roll out the taxi service around the US or further afield amid close regulatory scrutiny of driverless car technology.

As well as the Cybercab, Tesla is still ramping up production of its long-delayed Semi electric lorry. Musk is also aiming to produce one other new model: the Roadster sportscar, which Musk revealed with a demonstration of a “flying car” version that used thrusters developed by SpaceX to drive up a curved ramp before flipping and landing. #186. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#185. Iranians face looming war threat with no reliable info

Most people in Iran have little idea of the course of the US-led war and peace talks on the global stage. With few sources of information, the population must navigate conflicting rumors and fears of a nuclear attack.

"There is a constant sense of fear in the air," a 37-year-old mother in Tehran told DW. "Every time I hear a loud noise, I flinch. Even when a door slams, I jump — thinking that bombs are falling."

Now, unlike in the opening months of the war, her children are back at school.

"I don't work, but keeping the children at home out of fear is not a solution," she said. "They would go stir-crazy in our small apartment."

Schools remain open across Iran despite the military standoff with the US and Israel. However, some parents whose children attend private schools have received messages from those schools explaining what to do in the event of a renewed war or other emergency.

Numerous parents have shared such messages on social media.

Irans Education Ministry has tried to reassure the public.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"People should not pay attention to rumors spread with the aim of sowing fear and forcing schools to close," Ali Farhadi, a ministry spokesperson, said in a recent media interview.

Farhadi said the ministry would decide whether the schools stay open or close, and would do so in coordination with the security authorities. Should the security outlook change, the situation will be reassessed accordingly, the official said.

Parallel to Farhadi's appeal to disregard rumors aimed at raising fear, state media themselves are discussing scenarios of a possible nuclear attack.

On November 2, Iranian state television broadcast an advisory on protective measures in case of a nuclear strike. People were advised to remain in a shelter for at least 24 hours in the event of such an emergency.

Many in Iran fear that the United States is preparing to use nuclear weapons against the "Pickaxe Mountain" underground bunker about 220 kilometers (130 miles) south of Tehran. US President Donald Trump has hinted at attacking the location, which is close to Iran's Natanz nuclear facility, but made no explicit mention of using nuclear weapons.

Iran's government denies that any work related to its nuclear program is being carried out at the mountain bunker.

The fighting between the United States and Iran has mostly petered out in recent months as the Trump administration focused on the midterm election. But two days after the election, on November 5, the US news outlet Axios reported that the US military was making final preparations for a possible resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran.

At the same time, there are also hopes that a Democrat-controlled Congress would force Trump to scale down his military ambitions.

"It is still difficult to make any concrete assessment of the implications of the US midterm election results for the war with Iran," Hamidreza Azizi, the International Crisis Group's consulting senior Iran analyst, wrote in response to questions from DW.

Iran's government sees the election results as a victory, Azizi wrote. The regime's resistance to the Trump administration has contributed to the Republican Party's loss in the US midterms, and some in Tehran are already seeking to frame the result as a sort of revenge for the US-Israeli assassination of senior Iranian leaders in the opening stages of the war.

Against this backdrop, Iran is likely to take an even harder line on its core demands.

Trump has at least two months before the new Congress takes office, Azizi wrote. He could decide to resume strikes on Iran in an attempt to offset a domestic political setback by targeting a foreign policy victory.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Qatari mediators are trying to persuade the Iranian and US governments to agree on a draft peace deal. The aim is to prevent another round of escalation and pave the way for the resumption of direct talks in the coming days.

But even well-connected journalists in Iran have little information on the substance of the talks, which are closed to the public.

In a post on X on October 31, the Iranian journalist Hadi Mohammadi wrote: "Domestic media outlets are completely in the dark about negotiations that directly affect people's everyday lives. They have to wait for reports from Axios, Al Arabiya, Al Jazeera and other international media outlets. In such an environment, developing our own narratives and doing journalism becomes pointless."

As the fog of war persists, many in Iran no longer have the energy to keep up with the media reporting. A 72-year-old retired woman from western Iran told DW she now deliberately avoids the news.

"I hardly have the strength to think about it anymore," she said. "I'm just glad that my three children have emigrated."

Welcome to our live coverage of the US midterm elections – here are some of the latest key developments.

A number of closely watched contests in the midterms are still to be called, including the final two US Senate races – in Mississippi and Alaska. The Democratic candidates are hoping to oust Republican incumbents to bolster their new majority in Congress. Right now, Democrats have a 106-seat majority in Congress as we await final results.

Democrats flipped another eight House seats, strengthening their majority in the lower chamber. Democrats are now leading Republicans 253 to 157, with 25 races left to call, as a number of GOP representatives felt the weight of the blue wave that has swept their party out of power. Republicans held on to two House seats in the west as congressman Mike Kennedy won re-election in Utah and Amanda McKinney won in Washington.

Democratic socialist Nithya Raman was elected to serve as the mayor of Los Angeles, eking out a narrow win over incumbent Karen Bass, in a major shake-up in local politics that reflects the growing dissatisfaction with the direction of the city. The progressive urban planner had served on LA’s city council since 2020.

Harmeet Dhillon, a key Trump ally, resigned from her position leading the justice department’s Civil Rights division. Attorney general Todd Blanche said he accepted her notice. Dhillon is the first high-ranking justice department official to leave after the midterm elections. Democrats are expected to use their power in taking control of Congress to aggressively investigate executive agencies, including the justice department.

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect in Michigan, said the new majority in the upper chamber needed “action” from their leader. On the campaign trail El-Sayed refused to back Senator Chuck Schumer, who currently serves as the minority leader. The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the midterm results.

Donald Trump signed a proclamation that preserves the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments in his first official action after the Republican wipeout.

The US jobs report shows that employers added 165,000 jobs in October – a significant increase, defying expectations. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate saw a slight drop to 4.1%.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics is set to release the latest US jobs report at 8.30am ET today. Analysts have predicted a slight increase in October job numbers, while predicting that unemployment will stay around 4.2%.

A reminder that the last report before the midterm elections saw US employers add only 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from August’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly.

We’ll bring you the latest as we learn more.

European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market is poised for its worst day since March.

The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down 207 points, or 1.9%, at 10,575 points in mid-morning trading.

Germany’s Dax index fell by 1.9% in morning trading, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 1.5% and Spain’s Ibex lost 1.1%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”

Meanwhile, Donald Trump has issued a statement on his Truth Social app calling on US states to embrace artificial intelligence (AI), or “superintelligence” as he prefers to call it, arguing that those which attract AI companies, data centres and investment stand to become enormously wealthy. The post-midterms market rout has been particularly painful for Elon Musk.

Musk (who put $446m of support into Republican campaigns), has lost around $113bn of wealth in the last two days.

This is because his two largest companies have both been badly hit in the sell-off.

Tesla fell 3.34% on Wednesday, as investors reacted to the Democrats’ electoral success, then 10.7% on Thursday. Musk owns 17.7% of the carmaker.

SpaceX lost 3.8% on Wednesday, then 9% yesterday – which also hurt Musk as he owns 10.3% of it.

In total, Musk’s paper wealth fell by $33.5bn on Wednesday, and then by another $79.7bn yesterday, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

Despite this, Musk is still the world’s richest person with a paper wealth of $785bn, more than double Jeff Bezos in second place with $370bn.

Tuesday night’s explosive rout of the Republican party was supercharged by the fury of Hispanic Americans who turned out in record numbers in key battlegrounds to protest the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant assault on their communities.

“Trump went against us,” said Benny Melendez from Weslaco, Texas. “He made us the target of ICE operations, so we decided to punish him by voting against his party. That’s what happened.”

Melendez, the owner of a small housebuilding company in south Texas, voted for Donald Trump in the presidential election two years ago, attracted by his promise to secure the Mexican border and improve the economy. But on Tuesday, he cast his vote for the Democrats in a display of pure anger.

Two of his cousins and up to 15 of his building workers have been picked up and deported to Mexico by ICE. When Melendez voted for Trump in 2024 he expected the immigration raids would focus on those with criminal records, he said, not his relatives and employees.

“They’re taking our neighbors. They’re taking our friends. They’re they’re taking our workers, and they’re taking our family members. This is an attack against our community.”

Melendez’s rage, replicated in the millions across Texas, Florida and other critical swing states, itself tells a story. It speaks to how Trump first wooed, and then alienated, the backing of many Latino voters, effectively shooting himself in the foot.

#182. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#178. Commuters and shoppers face disruption from tube driver strikes in run-up to Christmas

RMT union calls eight 24-hour strikes on London Underground in opposition to plans for four-day week

Tube train drivers in the RMT union have called eight 24-hour strikes running over 16 days – including six in the lead-up to Christmas – that threaten to bring transport chaos to the capital.

The drivers will start another series of 24-hour strikes in late November in opposition to plans for a four-day week – a proposal that has been warmly welcomed by the majority of London Underground drivers represented by the Aslef union.

Disruption could mean few tube trains over the last shopping weekend before Christmas, with strikes running from noon on Thursday 17 December and again on Saturday 19 December.

The 24-hour strikes will begin at noon on 26 November, followed by the Christmas industrial action, with two more strikes planned in early January and more in February.

The RMT claims the new four-day week, which Transport for London (TfL) has said would be voluntary, would “undermine existing agreements and worsen working conditions”.

Previous strikes earlier this year resulted in widespread disruption to London Underground services, although trains ran on most lines.

The RMT said it has yet to receive guarantees about drivers’ right to remain on existing five-day working arrangements. It believes the proposals would worsen shift times and certainty.

The RMT’s general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said: “London Underground is attempting to dress up a wholesale attack on drivers’ working conditions as a voluntary four-day week.

“Our members are being asked to spend more time driving trains, accept longer and more unpredictable shifts and surrender agreements that have been negotiated and defended over many years.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

“This is not about improving work-life balance. It is about squeezing more work out of fewer drivers while giving management greater flexibility at the expense of our members.”

Similar, highly disruptive strikes took place in London in April and June, despite TfL insisting the proposals were completely voluntary, and the plans having been fully endorsed by the main drivers union, Aslef.

#177. Weeks before rape conviction, Russell Brand was featured speaker for Maha group allied with RFK Jr

Brand has been supported by Tony Lyons, who runs Maha Action, and has appeared on stage with Mehmet Oz

Weeks before Russell Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault by a court in the UK, he appeared as a featured speaker on a video call for Maha Action, an American group closely allied with the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr.

It was a reflection on the warm embrace Brand, a comedian and actor, has received from prominent Trump administration officials and other leaders in Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” (Maha) movement, where Brand has used his star status to criticize vaccines and vaccine mandates, junk food, and pharmaceutical companies. He has also heaped praise on Kennedy and other members of the Trump administration.

“You’ve just been a great force in the world and a great force for Maha,” Tony Lyons, who runs Maha Action and has close ties to Kennedy, said to Brand during that call in October. He also said at the time that he believed Brand was falsely accused. “We will stand up for you every week, week after week.”

Now, Maha must contend with Brand’s new status as a convicted rapist. He is due to be sentenced on Monday after being found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women. The actor and Christian influencer, who had pleaded not guilty to the charges, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator.

Brand was acquitted of two other rape charges and attempted indecent assault. It has also been revealed that he is now under investigation for two further rape allegations.

In the UK, Brand’s fall from star to convicted rapist centered on how the actor committed his crimes at the height of his fame. In the US, the trial did little to tarnish Brand’s standing in the Maha movement.

Among Brand’s most vociferous supporters has been Lyons, who runs Maha Action and other Kennedy-allied Maha groups, has close business ties to Kennedy, and published a book Brand wrote about converting to Christianity. Lyons accompanied Brand as he left court during his first week on trial, according to video captured by Reuters. On the Maha Action video call the following day, Lyons urged people to buy Brand’s book before tossing the call to Brand.

Lyons did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment in the wake of Brand’s conviction.

During the two Maha Action calls he joined during trial, Brand did not address the charges against him, but spoke about experiencing “the ceremonial pressure of a trial” and praised Kennedy, Mehmet Oz – another senior US health official – and others in the Maha movement. He has been involved with Maha Action since 2025 and has participated as a featured speaker on a number of the group’s calls. In one video call last year that included Oz, Brand dialed in while naked in a bathtub.

Brand was a moderator for a segment at the Maha Summit in September, at a daylong event that featured Kennedy, JD Vance and other Trump administration officials.

Brand and Oz kicked off their joint appearance together by making a joke about Brand touching a female member of Trump’s cabinet.

“Russell Brand was backstage hugging the secretary of agriculture, but here he is,” Oz told the crowd as Brand walked on stage. “Took Maha to a whole new level.”

“She initiated that contact, I should make clear, doctor,” Brand quipped in reply, prompting Oz to throw back his head, heartily laugh and slap both knees.

At the end of the segment, Kennedy, Oz and another health department official, Dan Brillman, joined Brand for photos in front of the audience.

Two weeks later, Brand’s trial began across the Atlantic Ocean.

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to messages seeking comment on the involvement of Kennedy, Oz and Brillman with Brand.

Brand is a British citizen, but moved to the United States before the 2024 presidential election.

His citizenship status in the United States is unclear. In a video posted in September 2025 by an immigration law firm, Brand provided an endorsement of its work, saying “when I become an American citizen” it will be because of the law firm.

Brand has recently referred to the US as “your country”.

“Your country has a lot of problems. Not as much as mine, as a matter of fact,” Brand said during the Maha Summit. “My country’s got some serious, serious problems.”

In the second Maha call he joined, during his trial on 21 October, as the midterm elections loomed, he thanked Lyons for his support.

“Even in a time of great adversity, knowing that I have your support, Tony, has been incredibly valuable,” Brand said. “This is a really important time for your country, a really important time for your movement in particular.”

#170. UK house prices fall at steepest rate in more than three years

October drop of 0.6% leaves average price of property at £296,285, says Lloyds, as high mortgage rates hit market

UK house prices fell at the steepest rate in more than three years in October, marking the fourth consecutive monthly decline, as high mortgage rates hit the housing market.

The average price of a typical UK property stood at £296,285 last month as prices unexpectedly dropped 0.6% compared with September, the steepest fall since the lender Lloyds recorded a 1.6% drop in August 2023.

Analysts had expected a small monthly rise of 0.1%, which would have marked the first monthly increase since June.

House prices were down 1.2% compared with the same month last year, the biggest annual fall since October 2023.

“Housing demand is currently being tested by a challenging economic backdrop,” said Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds. “Renewed inflationary pressures, driven in part by the conflict in the Middle East, are keeping borrowing costs high and adding to the squeeze on household finances, making some buyers understandably more cautious.”

Prospective buyers are facing increasingly high borrowing costs, with the average two-year fixed mortgage running at 5.97% and the average five-year fixed rate at 5.99%, according to the latest Moneyfacts market update.

The figures come a day after the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee put up the base rate by a quarter of a point to 4%, the first increase in three years, to fight inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war.

The conflict in the Middle East has driven the price of oil above $100 a barrel in recent months, resulting in soaring fuel prices and pushing inflation to 3.5% in September.

“The market has lost some momentum as we head towards the end of the year,” said Amy Reynolds, the head of sales at the Richmond estate agency Antony Roberts in London. “Buyers are still out there, but they’re being careful. The people hit hardest are those remortgaging and second-steppers trying to stretch to one more bedroom.

“The real damage is psychological. Another rise tells people that borrowing is getting more expensive, not cheaper, and that makes them hesitate.”

The property services company Savills this week said Britain’s sluggish housing market was not expected to recover until 2028, when a forecast improvement in the economy and mortgage affordability are expected to support a recovery.

While annual house price growth remains relatively strong in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, there is growing pressure in the south of England.

Greater London recorded the largest annual decline in October, with prices falling 3.1% year on year to an average of £524,892.

The capital was followed by the south-east and south-west of England, which recorded annual declines of 2.4% last month, to £379,258 and £298,057 respectively.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

On Friday the online property portal Rightmove downgraded its expectations of revenue and profit growth to the lower end of its guidance amid a slowdown in the housing market, in results for the four months to 31 October.

It said that high mortgage rates had resulted in buyer demand falling by 10%, with agreed sales down 9%, as record numbers of homes on the market led to “some downward pressure” on house prices.

Rightmove said there had been an increase in inquiries per property in the rental market, with prices up 2.9% year on year, but there were 6% fewer new homes on the website compared with the end of last year.

Last month, the Bank of England released figures showing that the number of home mortgage approvals fell to 53,443 in September, the lowest monthly figure since December 2023.

Last week, Nationwide reported that house prices flatlined in October, with the annual rate of growth dropping to the slowest in more than two years.

“The path back to growth runs through rate stability, and that road just got a little longer,” said Anthony Codling, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets. “On balance, this report is cautiously negative for near-term sentiment but does not signal a structural collapse.”

#169. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#166. Dogecoin jumps after Elon Musk replaces Twitter bird with Shiba Inu

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”

Elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”

It wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

The price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

#164. ‘Profound anger’ among black voters over Kemi Badenoch’s slavery remarks

Operation Black Vote chair says Tory leader’s claim that Britain should not apologise has caused ‘hurt and disbelief’

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay.

David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.

In a week in which the UK political agenda was dominated by postcolonial legacies, Badenoch said Burnham should not apologise for Britain’s historical role in slavery “because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash”, while criticising Commonwealth leaders on X.

Burnham, while saying he was open to making a formal apology on behalf of the British state, has ruled out reparations. Weaver said he welcomed the prime minister’s apparent willingness to apologise, but said the government’s “almost reflexive insistence” that any apology must come with assurances “reparations are off the table” was concerning.

Weaver said only the prime minister had the power to address the hurt felt by descendant communities and show Britain had the “moral courage to apologise without qualification”.

But he said Badenoch’s comments highlighted wider concerns about the UK’s political climate, adding: “At Operation Black Vote, we are hearing profound anger, hurt and disbelief.”

He added: “For us, this is not an abstract historical debate. It concerns our families, our heritage and our humanity. Political leaders should not underestimate the depth of feeling within black communities or their democratic power.”

Weaver said that in seeking an apology, Commonwealth nations wanted recognition of continuing colonial legacies that hampered development, and that Badenoch’s comments were “profoundly insulting”.

This week marked the second anniversary of Badenoch becoming the first black woman to lead a major British political party. OBV, a national, non-partisan civil rights group founded in 1996, welcomed her historic achievement in becoming Tory leader in 2024.

Meanwhile, although black voters were more likely than any other voters to have backed Labour in the 2024 general election, Weaver said OBV had found they felt “despondent” with the party and “taken for granted”, in particular over its handling of the consequences of the Windrush scandal.

Weaver added: “All parties should understand that to not apologise for slavery, the worst crime against humanity, is an insult. An apology should not have to be begged for. It should be an expression of genuine remorse and moral responsibility, not a carefully managed political statement designed to demonstrate toughness or avoid obligation.

“Reparative justice is not just about money. Ending an injustice does not erase responsibility for perpetrating it. We must ask why acknowledging this particular historical injustice remains so difficult and whether deeper racial attitudes continue to shape the debate.”

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

Badenoch, who has advocated a “colour-blind” approach to race, has long argued that people from ethnic minorities should be free to express differing views on race without being accused of betraying their communities. But while attempting to frame herself as a unifier, Badenoch has given roles to the hard-right politician Rupert Lowe, Katie Lam – the MP who said a “large number” of legal migrants “need to go home” – and the former neo-Nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, while outlining plans to scrap the public sector equality duty and leave the European court of human rights.

Weaver said: “She’s the leader of the Conservative party. That’s a big deal. She’s got a high popularity rating and can be very effective. But many black voters tell us there’s a lot of mistrust for her lack of empathy – and because she will sometimes say things her white counterparts could not say and get away with it. So she becomes the front for unacceptable views on race.

“The current state of public discourse – and the silence when it comes to challenging it – contributes to a sense among black communities that they are being treated with contempt across the political spectrum.

“This is not just about Badenoch. Just because you’re black doesn’t mean you have to hold a particular point of view. But your heritage, whether you are white or black, does not place your views beyond challenge. An apology for slavery is about humanity and decency and seeing people’s worth. Andy Burnham must do the right thing – and soon.”

Downing Street and the Conservative party were approached for comment. Commonwealth leaders have said the UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year.

#162. Global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels in 2026, likely the second-warmest year on record

Climate scientists say the world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius threshold in 2026. This year is also on track to become the second-warmest on record.

Global temperatures will almost certainly average more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels in 2026, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service said Friday.

That would make 2026 the second calendar year after 2024 above the threshold set as part of the Paris Agreement.

The Paris treaty was aimed at preventing global temperatures from rising above 1.5 degrees Celsius in the long term. The 2015 deal was seen as a major step forward in tackling climate change.

Most of the world's nations agreed to hold global temperature rise to well below 2 degrees Celsius compared to pre-industrial levels and "pursue efforts" to keep it below 1.5 degrees.

The target concerns long-term warming, so a single year above 1.5 degrees does not in itself mean it has been breached.

Copernicus estimates that 2026 will most likely be the second-warmest year after 2024 since records began. However, there is a 20% chance that it could surpass 2024 levels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The climate service also expects the four-year average for 2023 to 2026 to be above the 1.5 degree threshold.

October 2026 was the warmest October on record globally, with an average global surface temperature of 1.75 degrees above pre-industrial levels for the month. It marked the third consecutive month above the 1.5 degrees threshold.

"An exceptionally strong El Nino is adding further heat to a climate already warmed by human activities, while 2026 is on track to become the second calendar year above 1.5 degrees," said Samantha Burgess of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

The UN Environment Programme now expects warming to overshoot the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree target.

Because this threatens drastic climate extremes and dangerous tipping points, the overshoot should be kept as small and short as possible, it said.

According to a September report by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), every additional fraction of a degree makes the risks and impacts worse.

Climate scientist Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, called for temperatures to be lowered quickly again by removing CO2 from the atmosphere.

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 degrees Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It was now unavoidable that global warming would exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within the next five years, Rockström said at a briefing.

He said that humanity was currently on "a path to an unmanageable future."
